articles.title: A Cheesecake Factory joke fuels Trump and Obama's back-and-forth before midterms
articles.summary: With a week to go until the 2026 midterm elections , you'd be forgiven for thinking that President Trump and former President Barack Obama were running against each other this year. While campaigning for Democrats in Ohio over the weekend, Obama mocked the various renovation projects that Trump has been overseeing at the White House, prompting a pointed response from the president and his administration. "I don't know if you've noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovations," Obama told the crowd in Cleveland. "He should be on HGTV. Guy's building a ballroom that's bigger than the White House. He's paved over the Rose Garden. He's put a helicopter pad on the South Lawn. And there's gold everywhere — what's up with the gold? Everything, more gold. He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory." What else did Obama say? Obama also skewered the Trump administration for the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool controversy. "Remember that whole thing about 'drain the swamp'?" he said. "The only thing that got drained was the reflecting pool in the National Mall after some no-bid contract got it all messed up, and then they tried to blame a three-time Olympian and say he vandalized it." Obama also taunted Trump for starting a trade war with "that well-known evil empire, Canada." "I mean, these are the people who gave us maple syrup and Martin Short," Obama said. But it was the Cheesecake Factory line that seemed to strike a nerve with Trump . What was Trump's response? In a Truth Social post hours after Obama spoke, Trump called Obama a " grossly incompetent President " but did not address the Cheesecake Factory comment. On Monday, the White House account on X posted a digitally altered image of the restaurant's menu listing what it described as Trump's accomplishments, saying, "The only thing bigger than the menu is the list of President Trump's accomplishments." Then on Tuesday, the White House hosted an hourslong YouTube livestream titled "Lo-fi Beats to Dismantle DEI To," featuring a split-screen of what the administration described as Trump's efforts to dismantle DEI and an AI-generated cartoon of the president waving to a crowd of Americans in front of a Cheesecake Factory. A Cheesecake Factory in Naperville, Ill., in 2025. Timothy Hiatt via Getty Images At a campaign rally in Mississippi on Monday, President Trump praised the restaurant chain as "a very successful company" and defended the need for White House  renovations — which are projected to cost at least $900 million — while denying that he has spent too much time focusing on them. "The White House represents our country, and that has to be pristine," Trump said in Corinth, Miss., while stumping for incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. "I would try and explain that to a guy like Obama, but he wouldn't understand. He doesn't understand the White House has to be clean, pristine, beautiful. It can't have cracks in the column." Trump insisted that he had spent "very little time" on redesigning the White House, but also said that he has "fun doing it" and that "it actually relaxes me." "I do it very good," he said. "I'm really good in real estate and fixing things. I fix things very good, very beautifully and I always build beautiful and inexpensive, which is a good combination if you can do." Most Americans, though, disapprove of the president devoting his time to such projects. An ABC News/Washington Post poll conducted earlier this month found 59% of U.S. adults say Trump is spending "too much" time on renovating the White House, compared with 27% who say he is spending the right amount of time and 11% who say not enough. What's at stake? President-elect Donald Trump shakes hands with President Barack Obama during a meeting in the Oval Office, Nov. 10, 2016. Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images The president, whose overall approval ratings are near all-time lows, has been out on the campaign trail hoping to help Republicans avert a so-called blue wave and hold on to control of Congress. In recent stump speeches, Trump has urged would-be voters to pretend he's running to encourage a bigger turnout. "In this election, if you would, I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot," he said in Mississippi. Obama has been out on the trail too. He's seeking to boost Democrats in key races, such as those in Ohio and Michigan, as the party looks to flip both chambers of Congress. But Trump suggested Obama is campaigning against him. "He fought me with crooked Hillary [Clinton]. That didn't work out well. Then he fought me with Kamala [Harris]. That didn't work out well," the president said. "And now they say, 'Oh, whoa. Barack Obama is going to start campaigning.' And he's not even campaigning. Tell him he's not campaigning about me. Maybe he'll go home." articles.title: Supreme Court declines to restore judges' power to pause deportation cases
articles.summary: By Andrew Chung Oct 27 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court declined on Tuesday to reinstate the authority of immigration judges to temporarily postpone deportation cases, keeping in place an agreement between President Donald Trump's administration and Republican-governed Texas that bars the once-common practice. The justices denied ‌an emergency request by three US cities including Baltimore and an immigrant legal advocacy group to halt for now the deal ending the ‌practice, known as "administrative closure," while litigation continues in the dispute. The Supreme Court's decision, issued as a brief, one-sentence order, did not offer any explanation, as is common when it handles emergency requests. ​None of the justices publicly dissented from the decision. The administration and Texas filed the agreement in a federal court in Texas on June 22, the same day that the state sued to challenge the immigration court procedure. A federal judge swiftly approved the agreement on the same day. Baltimore and the other litigants said the federal government improperly colluded with Texas to secure the rule's invalidation. In a statement, the litigants and the lawyers representing them from the liberal legal group Democracy Forward expressed disappointment ‌in Tuesday's decision. "Eliminating these protections puts vulnerable people at greater ⁠risk of deportation and undermines public safety in communities across the country," they said in the statement. "This dangerous abuse of the judicial process threatens the rule of law and sets a troubling precedent for dismantling federal policies without meaningful public participation ⁠or judicial scrutiny," they added. Representatives from the Justice Department and the Texas attorney general's office did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Immigration judges relied on administrative closure for decades to clear certain deportation cases off their busy dockets, including when separate proceedings involving the same person are pending that could prevent removal, such as on a ​visa ​petition or an appeal of a criminal conviction. Critics including Texas and the Trump administration have ​said administrative closure has allowed immigrants who lack legal status ‌to remain indefinitely in the United States, acting in effect like an amnesty. HUNDREDS OF THOUSANDS OF CASES Administrative closure has been applied over the years in hundreds of thousands of deportation cases. Ending the practice is part of Trump's hardline approach toward immigrants. In 2024, Biden's administration adopted a regulation that formally codified administrative closure procedures, concluding that it lets judges efficiently manage their caseloads and promote the fair treatment of immigrants. That regulation replaced a prior rule adopted in 2020 during Trump's first term in office that had been judicially blocked. After Trump returned to office in 2025, the Justice Department office that oversees immigration courts, the Executive Office ‌for Immigration Review, announced it would not defend the Biden rule against a legal ​challenge. In a lawsuit, Texas argued that the rule lets immigration judges "effectively grant indefinite amnesty to aliens ​illegally present in this country." Trump's administration and the state then jointly ​asked US District Judge Reed O'Connor in Wichita Falls, Texas, to approve an agreement declaring the Biden rule unlawful. O'Connor did ‌so, blocking it permanently, nationwide. Three municipalities — Baltimore, New Haven, Connecticut, and ​Columbus, Ohio — and the legal services ​provider, Centro Legal de la Raza, sought to intervene in the case to defend the rule, but O'Connor rejected their bid. The cities say they all have substantial immigrant populations. The New Orleans-based 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals declined to put the agreement on hold pending an appeal ​of O'Connor's decision. The cities and Centro Legal de la Raza ‌told the Supreme Court in a filing that Trump's administration circumvented a federal law governing agency procedures by using "manufactured litigation" with "ideologically aligned" ​Texas to eliminate a regulation it disliked. "The need for interim relief is underscored by the collusion that infected this suit from its ​inception," they wrote. (Reporting by Andrew Chung in New York; editing by Will Dunham) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/us-supreme-court-denies-immigration-160948159.html

articles.title: Judge tosses new charges against ex-FBI officials in Hunter Biden case and criticizes DOJ
articles.summary: Washington —  A federal magistrate judge on Tuesday rejected the Justice Department's 11th-hour attempt to file new criminal charges against two former FBI counterintelligence officials, saying prosecutors could not take that step without judicial review first. In a tense exchange, Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia expressed shock and anger at the Justice Department for filing an unsworn and unsigned superseding complaint against the two FBI officials after midnight on Tuesday on the public court docket, noting it was never reviewed by him to establish whether there was probable cause a crime was committed. Filing an unsworn complaint on the public docket and bypassing judicial review, he said, is unheard of and raises questions about the DOJ's motivations. He said he would be ordering that the new version of the charging documents be "struck from the record," though the Justice Department could try to add new charges the proper way. The docket was later updated to say that the Justice Department's filings were entered "in error." "We have never had complaints filed that are unsigned," Faruqui said. "It is inappropriate. It harms the defendants." "I am unaware of that ever happening before in this court," he added. "I am frustrated that I got it in the middle of the night. But I am much more concerned that it is filed on the public record." John Borchert, a prosecutor from the U.S. Attorney's Office in Washington, D.C., conceded that the effort by the government to add fresh charges without judicial review in a criminal complaint was a first for him as well. He asked if Faruqui would agree to let the FBI agent who filed the affidavit in support of the new complaint swear and attest to his filing and then proceed with a hearing to determine if probable cause was met. Defense attorneys for the two ex-officials balked, with one calling such a move "Kafkaesque" and Faruqui analogizing such an action to simply serving as a notary. Faruqui accused the government of repeatedly making bizarre moves in the case that only raise concerns, saying it was like throwing gasoline on a fire, citing how the case was charged and the decision to use a special assistant U.S. attorney from out of town to help prosecute the case. "Everything you're doing is making me more and more concerned," he said.  "Why today on this one case have you changed the entire history of how you charge cases? It makes it look like the United States is afraid of me trying to find probable cause." "Let me address that squarely. We are not afraid of a probable cause finding," Borchert said. Faruqui said that while he was dismissing the superseding complaint with the new charge of obstructing a congressional proceeding, the court would still proceed with a preliminary hearing to determine whether the original criminal complaint charging them with lying to Congress , which was reviewed by a magistrate judge, meets the probable cause standard. Mary Dohrmann, one of Floris' attorneys, told the court that the changes between the original complaint and the new one the government tried to file were substantial and raised concerns about accuracy. "The evidence is mounting that this prosecution is about some political football, and not the law or the facts in this case," she said. Criminal complaints in felony cases are typically reserved for more exigent circumstances, such as ongoing threats to public safety or national security. And Justice Department guidelines and norms have typically urged prosecutors to avoid taking overt investigative steps on politically sensitive cases so close to a national election. Prosecutors filing an unsworn and unsigned superseding complaint overnight is likely to raise further questions about whether the case is politically motivated. "What is going on at the D.C. U.S. Attorney's Office? In the middle of the night, the government filed an unsigned and unsworn complaint attempting to fix the issues with their original charge against Ms. Floris and adding a new charge just as meritless as the first one," said Floris' legal team in a statement provided to CBS News. "In our combined decades of DOJ service, we have never seen or even heard of something like this being filed," the lawyers said. "That's because the public lodging of criminal charges must be authorized by the grand jury, a judge, or the defendant herself. Here, the government has taken that power for itself in a desperate attempt to delay our client's right to challenge the charges in court and litigate this case in the media, rather than the courtroom. We have asked to address this outrageous government conduct against a decorated public servant at today's court hearing." The allegations against Floris and Benavides The charges center on testimony that Floris and Benavides gave a congressional committee on July 19, 2023 and September 28, 2023, respectively. The superseding complaint alleges the defendants "knowingly and willfully provided materially false statements to the Committee about their respective awareness of and involvement in the FBI's investigations into Hunter Biden, and thereby corruptly obstructed, and impeded and endeavored to influence, obstruct, and impede the due proper administration of the law." The complaint is focused on statements they made in testimony concerning their roles on the Foreign Influence Task Force, and one of its counterintelligence operations known as "Round River," which was focused on collecting derogatory informant reporting on, among other things, Hunter Biden, to flag the reporting as Russian disinformation ahead of the 2020 election. Floris served as the deputy assistant director of the FITF from mid-2019 through mid-2022, while Benavides served as its section chief from mid-2019 through the 2020 election The complaint alleges that the defendants made false statements in their testimony "for the purpose of minimizing or concealing FITF's engagement with, and communications about, the Hunter Biden investigations and to impede the Congressional investigation." During the hearing, Ron Safer, an attorney for Benavides, cross-examined FBI special agent Bryan Witt over his communications with the House Judiciary Committee. Safer asked how he determined whether Benavides' alleged false statements were material to the committee's investigation and could have affected its decision-making. Witt acknowledged that the FBI was not permitted to directly question committee members or their staff, and that agents instead were required to submit written questions for the record — a method he said he had not experienced before in his career. He added that he had only interviewed Steve Castor, the general counsel for House Judiciary Committee Republicans, a day before Tuesday's hearing. "Nobody would know from reading that affidavit that you were limited in any way in your ability to question the staffers about materiality," Safer said. Prosecutors later told the judge that the FBI was limited in its interactions with the committee because of the Constitution's Speech and Debate clause, which insulates the legislative branch's deliberative process from the executive branch. When Safer pressed Witt further about the conversation with Castor and the written responses from the staffers, Witt admitted that Castor was not present for Benavides' testimony, nor had he reviewed the transcript. Witt also acknowledged that the staffers who reviewed the questions from the FBI were no longer with the committee, and he did not know if they had reviewed the transcript either. The hearing is expected to continue on Wednesday. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/hunter-biden-investigation-more-charges-filed-against-ex-fbi-officials/

articles.title: Alex Pretti's family says the DOJ is stonewalling their efforts for justice
articles.summary: Michael Pretti and Susan Pretti, parents of Alex Pretti, who was killed by federal immigration agents in January, listen during a news conference, Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, in Minneapolis. (AP Photo/Ellen Schmidt) - Ellen Schmidt/AP PROGRAMMING NOTE: Susan and Michael Pretti join CNN’s Jake Tapper on The Lead at 5 p.m. Eastern The parents of Alex Pretti , a US citizen shot and killed by immigration agents in Minneapolis in January, are accusing the Department of Justice of violating their rights under a federal victims’ rights law, as they demand transparency and justice in their son’s death. In a July letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche — obtained exclusively by CNN — an attorney representing Michael and Susan Pretti wrote they have not received any substantive updates from the DOJ regarding an investigation into their son’s death, and called the department’s attitude toward the case “cruel.” “The government’s pattern of conduct is not only unconscionable, but unlawful,” the letter states. Pretti’s parents on Tuesday accused the federal government of “shielding Alex’s killers” by not turning over the entire federal case file to state investigators. “We will no longer stay silent about the actions of the Department of Justice in the 275 days since Alex’s murder,” Pretti’s father, Michael, said in the family’s first news conference since the 37-year-old ICU nurse’s death. The Pretti family met with US Attorney for the District of Minnesota Dan Rosen on July 13, the letter explains, the same day Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty announced in a news conference federal officials had handed over volumes of evidence from Pretti’s shooting. However, the letter goes on to say that, despite a public acknowledgment from local officials of an evidence-sharing agreement, Rosen refused to provide any information and would not even confirm the arrangement. A gunshot perforation in a window pane can be seen in a window in front of a makeshift memorial for Alex Pretti on January 26 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. - Roberto Schmidt/AFP via Getty Images “It is impossible to convey how the government’s refusal to engage in transparent communication with the Pretti family has compounded their heartbreak,” the missive says. “Further, with each such refusal, U.S. Attorney Rosen even refused to explain the basis for his position, instead stating only that ‘I can’t tell you for all kinds of reasons,’ without providing a single one,” according to the letter. Federal investigators who briefly agreed to share their evidence with state law enforcement have since stopped cooperating , said Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison, who is leading a lawsuit against the Department of Justice. “We are in litigation with the federal government right now to secure the rest of the remaining file, which they could give us this morning if they were inclined to do so, but it looks like we’re going to need a court order. I’m sorry that it comes to that,” Ellison told CNN’s Sara Sidner Tuesday morning. “Any prosecutor can tell you, you can’t go forward with half a file. You need the whole thing.” CNN has reached out to the DOJ and the US Attorney for Minnesota. In its response to Minnesota’s lawsuit, the Department of Justice said it is not required to turn over evidence to a state agency before an active court case is underway. The Pretti family’s attorney, Steve Schleicher, says they have heard nothing from the DOJ since sending their letter. “I’ve never seen a family treated with such cruelty and disrespect,” he said. Pretti’s death was captured in its entirety on video. Like some other incidents that occurred as a result of the Trump administration’s ongoing immigration crackdown, the footage from Pretti’s shooting differed from the version of events provided by the Department of Homeland Security. unknown content item - Kristi Noem, then-DHS secretary, initially described Pretti as a “terrorist” who “attacked” officers after “brandishing” a weapon, though the video disputed those claims. White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller referred to Pretti as an “assassin” who tried to murder federal agents. “No one from the federal government called us on that horrible day, but they did go on TV to tell lies about Alex,” Michael Pretti said Tuesday. Video footage shows, minutes before the fatal encounter with Pretti, immigration agents patrolling a Minneapolis street and interacting with bystanders. A witness, Nilson Barahona, told CNN agents were trying to apprehend someone who fled into a donut shop that locked its doors, leaving the group of federal officers on the sidewalk and street. Agents detained one observer as others blew whistles, yelled and recorded video on their phones. Video shows Pretti attempting to intervene in a scuffle between an observer and the agents. During the incident, Pretti was pepper-sprayed in the face. One of the officers can be heard in the footage shouting: “Gun! Gun! Gun!” as Pretti is on his knees and bent forward. An agent removed Pretti’s gun from his waistband and can be seen exiting the skirmish. At about the same time, one agent drew his service weapon. About a second after the agent holding Pretti’s weapon moved away, the officer who drew his own weapon appeared to fire several shots at Pretti before another agent drew his weapon and a shot rang out. The other officer then raised his gun and fired more shots. At least 10 gunshots can be heard on the video. The DHS report on its initial investigation into Pretti’s death says an officer yelled, “He’s got a gun” multiple times before the officers fired. “It’s difficult to get up every day, to function, to be a parent, knowing that your child’s never coming home,” Susan Pretti told CNN’s Jake Tapper after Tuesday’s news conference. “No parent should have to live what we’re living. No daughter should have to wake up and know that her only sibling is no longer here.” “What the federal government has taken away from us, from his friends, his family, his colleagues, from his patients, from the patients’ families. They’ve taken away all of that — and it’s reprehensible,” he told Tapper. Susan Pretti said she knew Alex as her son, but the outpouring of support they’ve received from his friends and coworkers has helped her see another side of him. “Every letter and card that we received from his colleagues, telling us who he was, at work … not only helping his patients but his colleagues,” Susan Pretti said, choking up. “You know what that’s like for a parent to hear? It is probably the kindest thing a parent can ever hear about their child.” unknown content item - Michael Pretti said his trust in the government is fading. Pretti’s death followed the fatal shooting of Renee Good on January 7 and the non-fatal shooting of Julio Sosa-Celis on January 14 by immigration agents during Operation Metro Surge. Those incidents prompted significant protests in Minneapolis and across the country for weeks. Hennepin County prosecutors have fought the DOJ for key evidence in Pretti’s death for months, after federal law enforcement repeatedly threw up blockades to their access. On the day Pretti was killed, the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension attempted to access the scene to launch an investigation but was banned by federal authorities. CNN was on scene the next day when the BCA first accessed the scene on a court order from a state judge. State and local investigators sued the Trump administration in federal court to obtain evidence in Pretti’s killing. After an evidence-sharing agreement between the DOJ and Minnesota investigators was finalized in June, Hennepin County prosecutors received volumes of evidence in Pretti’s shooting. Weeks later, the DOJ abruptly changed course and stopped sharing information, leaving Hennepin County prosecutors unable to access crucial evidence such as the weapons used to shoot Pretti and the firearm Pretti was carrying in his waistband at the time of the altercation, according to court records filed October 13. People pay their respects during a candlelight vigil for Alex Pretti after he was shot and killed earlier in the day on January 24, in Minneapolis, Minnesota. - Brandon Bell/Getty Images/File The letter from Pretti’s parents asks the DOJ to identify the federal employees who shot and killed Pretti, commit to sharing information with state and local investigators, confirm whether the FBI is continuing to investigate Pretti’s murder, and return any items of Pretti’s personal property no longer needed for evidentiary purposes. “No family should have to beg the U.S. government to do its job,” the letter says. “And no government should act with such caprice.” The Pretti family’s attorney declined to say Tuesday whether they would file a suit of their own against the Department of Justice. “The family will avail itself to any and all remedies in its pursuit of justice for Alex,” Schleicher said. Until they find justice, the family is comforted by shared memories of their son. Michael Pretti recalled a specific camping trip when Alex was about 6 years old. Just as they were wrapping up the weekend and preparing to leave, Alex rode his new bike off a small bridge and into a creek. “He comes back and he’s soaked,” Michael Pretti said with a grin, prompting a chuckle from his wife. “That was a good memory, that was a good weekend that stands out,” he said, adding “that’s probably where his love for hiking and biking started.” CNN’s Andy Rose and Cindy Von Quednow contributed to this report. articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro and family will be granted visas after Brazil election loss, U.S. official says
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — A senior State Department official said Tuesday that Flávio Bolsonaro and his family will be granted U.S. visas after his weekend loss to incumbent Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in a hotly contested race that bucked a trend of conservative electoral results in Latin America. The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to visa privacy laws, said “the State Department will issue visas to Flávio Bolsonaro and his family and allow them entry into the United States.” Bolsonaro, who had President Donald Trump’s tacit support, had been under investigation for corruption, money laundering and tax evasion in Brazil and had been ordered to surrender his passport. The State Department official did not say if Bolsonaro had already left Brazil or if he and his family were en route to the U.S. A spokesperson for Bolsonaro did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday; his campaign manager Rogério Marinho also refused to comment. Bolsonaro’s brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, who lives in Texas, had publicly encouraged him to leave Brazil if he lost the election. Bolsonaro has touted his relationship with Trump and visited the White House in May. The family connections go deeper: Brother Eduardo Bolsonaro was convicted in absentia in June of illegally lobbying the Trump administration and sentenced to four years in prison. A warrant was recently issued for his arrest. Trump did not offer a full-throated endorsement of Bolsonaro in the runoff against Lula, as he has with some other right-of-center candidates in Latin America. But he suggested on Monday, without providing evidence, that Brazil’s election was “rigged.” Bolsonaro's decision to leave Brazil came as a deadline for him to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports expired at noon Tuesday. It remained unclear whether he had complied. Bolsonaro was served with the order to surrender his passports Monday, a day after his stunning loss . Bolsonaro said he received it outside the home where his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup following his 2022 election loss to Lula. After that defeat, Jair Bolsonaro fled Brazil for Florida . He returned three months later. The sealed Supreme Court order, viewed by The Associated Press, was issued Sunday. Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat and has made unsubstantiated allegations of election fraud. Bolsonaro raises questions about election he lost Bolsonaro initially asked for the election results to be annulled after an evening of chaos at some polling places that prompted authorities to extend voting by two hours. On Monday, he urged the electoral court to investigate alleged election fraud and nullify Lula's and Vice President Geraldo Alckmin's candidacies, which the electoral court has never done before. “I never thought about leaving the country,” Bolsonaro said in a video published on his social media channels. "I will hand over my passports and I will defend myself from this aberration. It is a clear attempt to intimidate me. But I will not be silenced." To overturn the result, Bolsonaro would have to present evidence of fraud affecting Lula's 4.4 million-vote margin and convince the eight-member electoral court before the results are certified on Dec. 18. Lula, who turned 81 on Tuesday, received more than 64 million votes, compared with fewer than 60 million for Bolsonaro, a margin of nearly 4%. Bolsonaro said in a video posted Monday on his social media channels that he had no plans to leave Brazil and instead was attempting to organize opposition among his congressional colleagues to the election results. His eight-year term as a senator expires Jan. 31, 2027, which will also cause him to lose special jurisdiction at the country's Supreme Court. Bolsonaro is under investigation by Brazil's Supreme Court for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion in two cases. In one, he's accused of using a sports betting company to launder fraudulent deductions from government pensions paid to senior citizens. In the other, he is accused of accepting millions of dollars from a disgraced banker . He has denied any wrongdoing in both cases, and has claimed Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who is heading one of the investigations, is a Lula ally. Prosecutors suspect the funds from the banker were used to pay his brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro’s, expenses and to promote Flávio Bolsonaro’s political agenda with the Trump administration, documents show. Mauricio Marcon, a lawmaker of Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party, also questioned de Moraes’ objectivity on Tuesday. “Seven minutes after the election, Alexandre de Moraes ordered his passports to be seized,” Marcon said. Bolsonaro "will represent us in a free country. He will continue to be our leader." Brazilians had earlier taken to social media to ask where Bolsonaro was. Reporters gathered outside his home in the capital, Brasilia, but he did not appear. A spokesperson for the Ministry of Security of Argentina denied reports the Brazilian senator had entered the country. Brazilian media outlets reported that many Bolsonaro allies had been unable to reach him. Paulo Figueiredo, a close ally of Bolsonaro's who lives in the United States, was asked about the senator's whereabouts and did not answer directly. “At this moment — following months of intense work that were unfairly thwarted — I have no desire to speak with the press. I kindly ask that you do not persist. Should I have a statement to make on any matter, I will reach out,” Figueiredo said. ___ Savarese reported from Sao Paulo, Brazil. articles.title: Utah authorities connect serial killer Ted Bundy to another 1970s homicide
articles.summary: DNA connects serial killer Ted Bundy to the death of another Utah teenager, authorities announced Tuesday, exactly 52 years after her body was discovered in the woods by a hunter. Bundy has been dead since 1989, but the tally of his confirmed victims continues to grow due to advances in DNA testing. He killed at least 30 women and girls in multiple states in the 1970s, and many more escaped or survived with injuries. Investigators are satisfied that Bundy was responsible for killing 17-year-old Melissa Ann Smith in 1974, a death that had long been listed as a cold case, Summit County Attorney Margaret Olson said at a news conference. They were able to close the case by making crucial connections with DNA found on Smith and Laura Aime, another Bundy victim whose case was resolved last April in Utah County. Bundy's DNA was on file in Florida, where he was convicted and ultimately executed. Besides that evidence, Smith’s death showed hallmarks of Bundy’s “pattern, motive, means and opportunity,” Olson said. Utah's state crime lab got new technology in 2023 that extracts DNA from samples even if they are small, degraded from age or contain DNA from multiple people. “This case demonstrates the importance of preserving evidence,” said Salt Lake County Sheriff Rosie Rivera, whose department has also investigated homicides linked to Bundy. “We have to solve these cases to the best of our ability,” she said, explaining the importance of tapping science, even so many years later. "Nobody is just going to walk away and just blame everything on Ted Bundy, even though many cases have been that way. Here in the state of Utah, we take it very seriously.” Smith's relatives were contacted about the findings but declined to attend the news conference and declined to speak to reporters, the Summit County Sheriff's Office said. “With every case closure, may we stomp the memory of Ted Bundy out,” Utah County Sgt. Mike Reynolds said. Bundy was executed by electric chair in Florida for the 1978 murders of two women at the Chi Omega sorority house at Florida State University. He gave a series of confessions in his final days, including to some crimes that were previously unknown to police. Not all of those cases have been confirmed. Besides Florida and Utah, authorities said Bundy had victims in Colorado, Idaho and Washington state. They said they're especially working to solve the 1974 death of 16-year-old Nancy Wilcox of Utah. Solving the Smith homicide “does not close the book on Ted Bundy,” said Det. Ben Pender of the Salt Lake County Sheriff's Office, which has the Wilcox investigation. “Information kind of leads to Ted Bundy but again we're not for certain on Nancy Wilcox. We're going to continue to work that case." This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/utah-authorities-connecting-serial-killer-152942415.html

articles.title: 3 Alexander brothers each get 30 years for sex trafficking after women speak in court
articles.summary: Real estate brokers Oren and Tal Alexander and their bother Alon listen as their lawyers argue for a lesser sentence on their behalf at a New York courtroom on Tuesday. (Jane Rosenberg / Reuters) Two former luxury real estate brokers and their brother were each sentenced to 30 years in federal prison, seven months after they were convicted of drugging and raping women in a sex trafficking ring. Federal prosecutors sought life sentences for Oren and Alon Alexander, a pair of former powerful real estate brokers, and their brother, Tal, in a New York City courtroom Tuesday afternoon. Attorneys for the brothers, who have asserted their innocence, asked the judge to give the men the mandatory minimum instead. U.S. District Judge Valerie Caproni characterized the brothers as “Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde.” On one side they were described as gentlemen who loved their children, she said, and on the other described as “sadistic, misogynistic, sexual predators.” “Your conduct was monstrous,” Caproni said in her sentencing. But Caproni added that she did not believe the Alexander brothers were beyond redemption, declining the request to give them life sentences. In addition to 30 years of incarceration, the judge ordered 10 years of supervised release and sex offender treatment approved by the probation office. They are not to have contact with any child under the age of 18 unless approved by the probation office. Twins Alon and Oren Alexander, 39, were ordered to pay $300,000 each in fines. Tal Alexander, 40, was ordered to pay $350,000. Caproni said that she will ask the Bureau of Prisons to consult with experts as to whether they should be allowed to be held together as she believes they are bad influences on each other. The men were found guilty in March of 10 counts, including conspiracy to commit sex trafficking and sex trafficking by force, after a trial that included testimony from 11 women who described being lured, drugged and sexually assaulted over a period of years. Six of the women were part of the indictment. Tal Alexander and Oren Alexander in New York in 2016. (Sean Zanni / Patrick McMullan via Getty file) In a sentencing memo, prosecutors in New York’s Southern District said more than 70 women came forward with allegations of abuse and accused the brothers of exploiting their wealth, influence and connections to target victims. Victim statements from 11 women, some using court-assigned pseudonyms, were read at the hearing prior to the judge’s decision. The women asked the judge to impose a sentence that was appropriate for the profound impact the men had on their lives. One victim, Maya Miller, described the trauma of her rape by Tal Alexander as having settled into her nervous system. “I carry a quiet funeral inside me,” Miller said. Another victim, Olivia Lane, told the judge that she was “profoundly incapacitated” and after having a fraction of one drink while meeting Oren Alexander. She described being raped at least a dozen times while being terrified and in pain. She then directly addressed the men. “You are weak, you are inhumane,” Lane said. “You never had power and look at you now.” Two women described the men as having almost inhuman eyes during their assaults. Isa Brooks said, “Their eyes went black during the attack like I was being mauled by animals.” Lane said, “I remember looking at him and seeing a monster, black eyes.” The women also emphasized the Alexander brothers’ lack of remorse or acknowledgment of their victims throughout the trial. Victim Katie Moore noted in her statement that after five weeks of trial and being found guilty, the men “cannot even look us in the eye as we speak today.” “These men spent years treating women and girls like their humanity meant nothing,” Moore said. The brothers honed their methods together, attacking women in a way that was designed to humiliate and degrade them, prosecutor Elizabeth Espinosa said at the sentencing. “When they were done, they bragged to each other and their friends ... the defendants knew exactly what they were doing and they did it anyway and they did it over and over and over again,” Espinosa said. Oren Alexander, 37, center, and his twin brother, Alon, center-right, speak to their attorney Joel Denaro during their bond hearing at the Richard E. Gerstein Justice Building on Dec. 13, 2024, in Miami. (Matias J. Ocner / Miami Herald via Getty file) At trial, prosecutors said the brothers raped the women after having promised them parties and trips. One woman testified that she lost control of her body after she had a drink with Alon Alexander at a New York City club. When she awoke, she testified, they were naked on a bed. She kept trying to get up, and he kept pushing her back down, she said. When she told him that she didn’t want to have sex with him, she testified, he responded, “‘You already did.’” In a sentencing submission, attorneys for the brothers acknowledged that they sometimes behaved insensitively toward women but categorically denied that any of them had raped or sexually assaulted anyone. At trial, the attorneys described the sex as consensual and said the women were motivated in part by financial gain. “All the stories were rehearsed,” Tal Alexander’s attorney, Deanna Paul, said in her closing argument. “They’re looking for money.” Paul urged the judge to consider giving her client the mandatory minimum of 15 years in prison, saying that the jury’s verdict has not changed the attorney’s view of the evidence. The defense lawyer said that 15 years is already an extraordinary punishment, so “what would another 20 or 30 years accomplish?” Attorneys for the other two brothers similarly asked the judge to give the men 15 years. Marc Agnifilo, who represents Oren Alexander, told the judge that the men all stopped their “sexually aggressive” behavior after meeting their wives. “All three defendants stopped, and that matters,” Agnifilo said. Each of the brothers were given an opportunity to address the court directly before he issued his sentence. Oren Alexander was the first to ask the judge for a lighter sentence. He once again denied the assaults in his comments before telling the judge that he has built a new life and family. “My son needs me and I need to be there for him and I ask your honor to impose the minimum sentence,” he said. Tal Alexander was next to speak and expressed regret over his past actions. “The person who stands in court is not the same man as before,” he said, asking the judge to consider the entirety of his life in the decision. “I wish I showed more maturity,” he said. “I cannot undo moments when I was immature and careless with other people’s feelings. I understand the jury found me guilty and I know words cannot change that.” The last brother to speak, Alon, insisted that he was innocent and that he had never raped any women. He invoked his two young daughters when asking for the mercy of the court. “I am afraid of being Daddy in the photograph,” he said. Caprio appeared unmoved by their statements, emphasizing that the rapes were not a result of “party culture or hookup culture” as they described. The judge noted that it was not enough to rape the women, the brothers sought to humiliate them. “That marriage would transform them from sexual predators to normal gentlemen, I disagree,” Caprio said. “Rape is about power ... having a girlfriend or a wife doesn’t mean you are not going to rape or humiliate women.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/ex-luxury-real-estate-brokers-brother-sentenced-federal-sex-traffickin-rcna605818

articles.title: Trump could set off a Senate showdown if a Democrat wins in Alaska
articles.summary: Senators are bracing for a potential floor fight over accepting the results of the Alaska Senate race between incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) and former Rep. Mary Peltola (D) — and perhaps other battleground contests — if President Trump urges allies to dispute what he might view as unfair or “rigged” results. Democratic senators generally view Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) as a straight shooter who would be averse to rejecting an election result in an Alaska Senate race certified by the governor and lieutenant governor. But they aren’t ruling out the possibility that the president will prod his MAGA allies in the Senate to contest the election results if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses by a narrow margin and blames his loss on voter confusion leading to a significant number of votes for his opponent with a similar name, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. If Alaska’s top officials certify Peltola as the winner, and Trump calls on Senate allies to reject that finding, it puts Thune in a tough spot and potentially sets up a messy floor fight. “Everybody is gaming everything out, and everybody is preparing for everything,” a Senate Democratic aide said of the preparations for potential Republican objections if Peltola narrowly beats the incumbent Republican senator. Sarah Binder, a professor of political science at George Washington University and a Senate rules expert, said Trump’s aggressive threat to challenge a Democratic win in Alaska could lead to a nasty Senate floor fight. “We can’t rule anything out at this stage just given the president’s single-minded persistence that there’s a lot of electoral fraud conducted by Democrats,” she said. “Would he push Republicans to object to the seating, if Alaska certified the seating of Peltola? The second question is, if he did that, would Republicans actually follow through?” Binder continued. “That gets us into the hornet’s nest of what the Senate would do to challenge a literal swearing in,” she added. “There’s no single charted pathway here.” She noted that, historically, if Alaska certifies Peltola as the winner over Sen. Dan Sullivan, Republicans could object to swearing her in. “I could imagine a scenario where they would want to swear her in, and somebody objects,” she said. Senate sources familiar with how the floor process would play out said that a Trump-allied senator or a group of GOP senators could signal an intention to object to Peltola — or to the Democratic winner of another close Senate race where Trump might claim election fraud — taking the oath of office to become senator in 2027. That would then lead to a negotiation between Thune and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) over how to resolve the situation. Senate Republican sources say they’re confident that incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan will defeat Peltola next week. Recent polls show Peltola leading the GOP senator by 2 percentage points, but the race is within the margin of error. Recent surveys by Data for Progress, InsiderAdvantage and Alaska Survey Research showed the Democrat leading by 2 points while a New York Times/Siena poll conducted from Sept. 24 to Oct. 1 showed her ahead of Sullivan by 7 points. Alaska has ranked-choice voting, which could shift how some votes are counted. One relevant Senate precedent comes from January 1997, when Republican candidate Woody Jenkins petitioned the Senate to throw out Democrat Mary Landrieu’s victory in the 1996 Senate race in Louisiana. Landrieu won by more than 5,000 votes, but Jenkins alleged “widespread vote tampering.” Senate leaders resolved the matter by agreeing to seat Landrieu “without prejudice” and referring the allegations of election fraud to the Senate Rules Committee to investigate. The deal left open the door to the Senate voting to unseat Landrieu by a majority vote if the charges of cheating were substantiated. In the end, the Rules Committee voted unanimously in October 1997 to end its investigation and clear Landrieu of wrongdoing even though it acknowledged some voting irregularities. Trump is laying the groundwork for a similar fight this fall if Peltola wins, giving Democrats a crucial pickup in a GOP-leaning state. The Trump Justice Department last week asked a federal court to block the certification of the winner of the Alaska Senate race if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses by a narrow margin and could argue that he would have won if his near-namesake, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., hadn’t been on the ballot. Legal experts have broadly dismissed the Justice Department lawsuit as meritless, raising the prospect that Trump’s next move may be to demand that GOP senators refuse to seat Peltola if she wins by a small margin. “They’ve set up the argument already that there’s a deliberate deception on the part of the other Dan Sullivan, and even though this seems to have been adjudicated in Alaska law, they will certainly argue the issue of fairness remains,” said Steven S. Smith, a professor of political science at Arizona State University, who follows Senate politics. Alaska’s Division of Elections, which is led by the state’s Republican lieutenant governor, initially removed “Dan J. Sullivan” from the ballot, but a state judge later ruled that he be placed back on the ballot. The Alaska Supreme Court upheld that decision . To avoid confusion, the Alaska ballot lists “Dan S. Sullivan” as the Republican incumbent and lists his opponent as “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” without party affiliation. Given that the Alaska Supreme Court has already ruled that the little-known Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. deserves a spot on the ballot, it would be hard to see how state officials could withhold the certification of a narrow Peltola victory without being overturned by the courts, legal experts say. That then sets the stage for a fight in the Senate, where any number of Trump allies or ambitious Republican senators who are looking for a springboard for national publicity could object to seating Peltola. “This is really a question of Trump-backed Republicans, and I think with Trump probably urging them to exploit every opening, the certification of the Democrat will lead to a Republican challenge if they’re in a position in the Senate to do so,” Smith said. If Peltola wins her race by a narrow margin, however, she will need Alaska’s Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy and Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom, who handles the duties of the secretary of State, to certify her victory. If Republican state officials refuse to certify a Peltola victory, then Senate Republicans argue the Senate rules would not allow the upper chamber to seat her when the Senate convenes for the new Congress on Jan. 3. The matter would need to be resolved by Alaska’s courts. A similar stalemate played out in 2009 after the close contest between Democrat Al Franken and GOP Sen. Norm Coleman in Minnesota. The state’s Republican Gov. Tim Pawlenty signed the election certificate validating Franken’s victory only after the Minnesota Supreme Court unanimously ruled in June 2009 that Franken had won the race by just more than 200 votes. Democrats, who had 59 seats at the time, agreed not to seat Franken until the legal process played out. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. All rights reserved. articles.title: Missouri voters protected abortion rights in 2024. Now they're voting on it again.
articles.summary: Just two years after Missouri voters approved an amendment enshrining the right to reproductive freedom in the state constitution, abortion, which was also protected by the measure, is on the ballot there again. On Nov. 3, Missouri residents will be voting on Amendment 3, only this time it would prohibit abortion, except in cases of medical emergencies, fetal anomalies, rape or incest. If the abortion is due to rape or incest, the procedure must occur no later than 12 weeks' gestation. Since Roe v. Wade was overruled by the Supreme Court in June 2022, 13 states have ceased nearly all abortion services while four states have a six-week ban on books, according to an ABC News tally. Missouri lawmakers move to repeal abortion protections enacted by voters Following the Supreme Court decision, Missouri enacted a trigger ban, prohibiting most abortions in the state. However, in November 2024, Missouri became the first state to overturn a near-total abortion ban through a direct vote of the people by passing Amendment 3 -- the same name as the upcoming ballot measure -- with about 52% of the vote. "Missourians have access to abortion care because the people made it possible," Mallory Schwarz, executive director of the nonprofit Abortion Action Missouri, told ABC News. "But not even months after our 2024 vote, politicians started plotting to overturn the will of the people and now, in a couple of weeks, voters will have to vote again to protect the right to abortion that we enshrined in the constitution previously." David A. Lieb/AP Photo, FILE - PHOTO: In this May 14, 2025, file photo, abortion-rights activists protest in the Missouri Capitol in Jefferson City, as the state Senate approves a proposed constitutional amendment to restrict abortion. What is Am e ndm e nt 3? Amendment 3 would repeal the 2024 amendment that granted reproductive freedom, including abortion through fetal viability, which is typically between 24 and 26 weeks' gestation. If approved, the amendment would also permit state lawmakers to enact legislation to regulate abortions and access to care. Examples include laws requiring physicians providing abortion care to have admitting privileges at a nearby hospital and licensing requirements for abortion facilities. State Sen. Adam Schnelting, who sponsored the proposal that led to Amendment 3 being placed on this year's ballot, told ABC News that passing the amendment is "critical to protecting women and children and providing Missourians with a measure that is more in line with their values than the one narrowly passed two years ago." The amendment would also prohibit gender-affirming care procedures, cross-sex hormones or puberty-blocking drugs for minors. However, gender-affirming surgeries and medical treatments for minors are already illegal in Missouri under statutory law. Opponents of the amendment have argued that including language about gender-affirming care is an attempt to mask the parts of the amendment that would limit abortion care. "What politicians are trying to do is mislead voters and overturn the will of the people and ban abortion again," Tori Schafer, an attorney for the ACLU of Missouri, told ABC News. "And they've shown they're willing to resort to all kinds of tricky tactics in order to do that." Schafer said organizations supporting Amendment 3 don't use the word "abortion" in their ads campaigning for the amendment to pass "because they know, like we know, that abortion care is popular in Missouri." Schnelting said the statutory ban on gender-affirming procedures and treatment for minors expires in 2027 and including that language in Amendment 3 would ensure such a ban is permanent. The ACLU of Missouri said the sunset clause only pertains to hormone therapy and that surgery is currently banned in Missouri. Fighting for their lives: Women and the impact of abortion restrictions in post-Roe America Possibl e cons e qu e nc e s if Am e ndm e nt 3 is pass e d After the trigger ban was passed in Missouri in 2022, the state's last abortion clinic in St. Louis was forced to stop providing such care . In 2023 alone, more than 12,000 Missouri women traveled to neighboring states, including Illinois and Kansas , to receive care, according to the Guttmacher Institute, a reproductive rights organization. Additionally, in 2025, more than 3,000 Missourians obtained medication abortions through telehealth from out-of-state clinicians, nearly four times higher than two years prior, the Guttmacher Institute found. Some abortion providers told local news outlets they were seeing patients develop complications while waiting for treatment and some patients said they'd had to flee Missouri to seek abortion care for conditions including fetal anomalies. "Missourians have lived under an abortion ban in the past," Schwarz said. "We've seen people turned away from the emergency room when they needed emergency abortion care. We've seen women forced to wait until their complication was serious enough that they were able to access care or have to flee the state to get care in another state that they should be able to get in their own community." Schwarz said Abortion Action Missouri's canvassers have had conversations with Missourians against Amendment 3 from all walks of life. One such conversation was with a Catholic voter who said they did not support abortion rights but also did not support the new amendment. "They said, 'I'm personally pro-life, but we already voted on this and I'm voting "no" this time because politicians should be listening to the people,'" Schwarz said. "'Politicians shouldn't get to overturn any vote just because they don't like it.' And so, we are hearing that [at] the doors every day, every weekend." A state-by-state breakdown of where abortion stands after ballot initiatives pass Schnelting said the response to Amendment 3 from his constituents has been largely positive and called the claims that it is overturning the will of the people a "specious argument." Anti-abortion rights groups have praised the new Amendment 3, arguing that the 2024 vote was extreme and goes beyond what Missourians have historically supported. "Despite what voters were sold before Election Day, as soon as [2024's] Amendment 3 passed, the abortion lobby brought litigation to perform late-term abortions, end parental consent and remove every safety regulation on their industry," Marjorie Dannenfelser, president of Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, said in a statement last year. "Amendment 3 is far too extreme and dangerous." Missouri is not the only state with abortion on the ballot on Nov. 3. Voters in three states -- Idaho, Nevada and Virginia -- will consider measures to protect abortion rights and, in some cases, reproductive freedom. Schafer, from ACLU of Missouri, said other states can learn from Missouri about how access to abortion can be at risk even after voters vote to protect care. "While this fight is really important to folks like me who live in Missouri and have to suffer the consequences of our legislature ignoring the will of the people, we know that this campaign will also impact folks all across the country," Schafer said. "We have friends in other states who have passed their own versions of the right to reproductive freedom, and we don't want this attempt by our legislature to embolden this opposition strategy across the country." She went on, "So we know that a lot of eyes are on Missouri, and Missourians deeply believe in the right to make their own decisions free from political interference." articles.title: Trump-backed senator warns Republicans could lose the Senate over 1 state
articles.summary: WICHITA, Kan. — Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., knows that he’s running for his political life, even in deep-red Kansas, where a Democrat hasn’t won since the Great Depression. It’s a Senate race that, until just a few months ago, was not on national Republicans’ radar. But Adam Hamilton, a well-known megachurch pastor styling himself as a moderate, has made the race uncomfortably close for Marshall and the GOP and pushed what was once a safe bet into toss-up territory. In an interview with Fox News Digital in Wichita, Kan., hours before President Donald Trump was set to rally behind the embattled incumbent, Marshall acknowledged that if he falls, Democrats may very well gain control of the Senate. Sleeper Senate Race Emerges As Unexpected Headache For Republicans Ahead Of Midterms President Donald Trump and Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., attend a campaign event in Park City, Kansas, on Oct. 19, 2026. "I think that, you know, I'm not a political expert, I'm a physician, but if we lose Kansas, I don't see how we keep control of the Senate," Marshall said. "And that's why a vote for Adam Hamilton is a vote for Chuck Schumer and Democrat control of the Senate. It’s that simple." Republicans are trying to maintain, and even grow, their slim, 53-seat majority in the upper chamber. Kansas, which hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in nearly a century, wasn’t supposed to be a problem. Read On The Fox News App But political experts on the ground contend that Hamilton’s uniqueness as a candidate — he’s been a prominent figure in Kansas for roughly three decades leading the massive Church of the Resurrection — and the political headwinds associated with Trump have created an ideal environment for Marshall to lose. "I can't imagine how factors could be any better for Democrats than they are this election cycle," Don Haider-Markel, a professor of political science at the University of Kansas, told Fox News Digital. "The last time it seemed to be close at all was 2020, and that race ended up not being as close." Dem Senate Hopeful Rejects Schumer But Benefits From Millions In Spending By His Allies That was Marshall’s first race for the Senate, where he won by nearly 12 points with Trump at the top of the ticket. But as Haider-Markel and others have pointed out, midterm elections are typically a check on the party in power, and Trump is not on the ballot this year, though that’s a reality he implored Kansans to ignore during his rally in Park City, Kansas. "In this election, I'm asking you to pretend please that I'm on the ballot," Trump said. "Just pretend." Still, voters in Kansas are dealing with affordability issues and high fuel prices , a point that Marshall admitted was why his race was much closer than outside observers initially predicted. "Look, it's the price of gas, and I do feel people's pain," Marshall said. "Every year I go to all 105 counties, finish up the 105 counties in June, and as that price of gas went up, I felt more and more frustration." "So maybe we're up 12 points before the Iran war, and as the price went up our poll numbers went down, so I think it's the price of gas," he continued. Along the asphalt and concrete arteries that connect Hamilton’s home base of Overland Park, Kansas, to what would be, for a brief moment, the center of the MAGA universe in Wichita, neon signs sprouting from gas stations almost all showed fuel prices that hovered just below $4 for gas and well over $6 for diesel . Trump Voters Reveal Their Biggest Fear Heading Into Midterms — And It's Not Rising Prices Democrat senatorial candidate Adam Hamilton answers questions from the media after a televised debate with Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., at WDAF studios in Kansas City, Mo. Nathaniel Birkhead, a professor of political science at Kansas State University, argued that high gas and diesel prices were certainly a contributing factor to Marshall’s struggles, but not the only one. Birkhead told Fox News Digital that it was Marshall’s tight connection to Trump at a time when the "Trump Brand is not particularly popular" has left an opening for a Democrat like Hamilton to enter the fray. "So we have this kind of contrast of Hamilton benefiting from kind of a down year for Republicans. But then also, again, the fact that Marshall is really kind of tying himself to Trump rather than trying to kind of separate himself," Birkhead said. "I think if this had been Jerry Moran running instead of Roger Marshall, I think it'd be far less competitive." Click Here To Download The Fox News App Therein lies the conundrum for Marshall and Republicans — they know that they need Trump’s support and his loyal base of voters, but they have to walk a fine line to capture other Republican voters and independents that might sit this election out or vote the other way. And that’s the crux of Marshall’s argument: without MAGA voters, he can’t win. "Look, I'm the doctor always weighing the benefits and risks of everything. And I'm telling you, we don't win this election without Trump voters getting out and voting," Marshall said. "The majority of the undecideds are Trump supporters. And they need to hear from him, 'Here's the plan, and this is how we're going to bring those prices back down, that if we leave Democrats in control, the price of the gas will never go down.'" articles.title: “新美联储通讯社”：美联储高层爆发路线之争，沃什的"沉默策略"能走多远？
articles.summary: 美联储内部就沟通策略产生分歧，沃什"少说话"路线遭同僚“抵制”。 10月27日，“新美联储通讯社”Nick Timiraos撰文指出，美联储主席沃什力推"沉默即美德"的新沟通风格，却未能说服多数同僚跟进，导致委员会对外传递出嘈杂而分散的信号，令市场在短短一个月内对10月加息的预期概率从70%骤降至15%。 文章统计，在上次政策会议结束至本周会议静默期开始之间，16位任期满一年的美联储官员合计发表了不少于59场演讲、采访及公开表态，与一年前同期的约54场大体相当。 这一数字表明，尽管沃什今年5月就任主席后刻意压缩自身发言，其他官员却纷纷填补空缺，各自阐发观点。 上述分歧产生的直接后果已在市场上清晰呈现。美联储上月加息后，市场从沃什的新闻发布会言辞中推断连续加息的可能性较高；其后两位副主席相继表态，暗示并不急于立即行动，10月加息概率随即大幅回落。 全国互助保险公司首席经济学家Kathy Bostjancic表示： 如果沃什不开口，其他人就会填补这个空白。 沟通路线之争：是否告知市场"反应函数" 这场争论的实质，并非是否恢复承诺式前瞻指引——几乎没有官员希望重回2021年前那种做法，彼时过于明确的利率承诺被认为拖延了美联储对通胀的应对。 文章指出核心分歧在于：官员是否仍应向公众解释，自己将如何响应经济变化？ 沃什的立场鲜明。他认为，持续叙述政策展望会将官员锁定在自身预测之中，同时模糊市场能够向美联储反映的信号。他本月在曼谷表示： 我不打算现在就说我在今年剩余会议上可能会做什么，这是美联储的新篇章，我们不再做这种事了。 支持这一立场的里士满联储主席Tom Barkin也对记者表示，自己"非常乐见这似乎正在成为机构惯例"。Barkin一贯谈论经济形势，但几乎从不就具体会议表态。 反对声音：不解释框架只会"制造噪音" 然而，多位官员公开为更充分的沟通辩护。 克利夫兰联储主席Beth Hammack 本月发表演讲指出， 如果家庭或企业"在对政策走向存在错误判断的情况下进行借贷，代价可能十分高昂"。 她在接受采访时强调，阐明自身思维框架并不等同于做出承诺： 他们听到的不是承诺，因为我没有给出承诺，我是在解释一个框架。 圣路易斯联储主席Alberto Musalem 在伦敦的讲话中直接驳斥"少说话可以让市场专注于数据"的逻辑， 称一家对自身框架守口如瓶的央行"并不能让市场聚焦于数据，猜测只会制造噪音"。 他补充道： 摆在央行面前的选择不是在嘈杂的过度承诺与沉默寡言之间二选一，而是在让公众自行猜测与主动告知之间做出抉择。 Hammack与Musalem均于2024年出任现职，两人均来自金融业背景，今年以来也始终是主张进一步加息的代表性声音。 "实验"遭遇现实检验，前官员提出警示 这场沟通实验在上月加息后迅速遭遇压力测试。 Nick Timiraos指出，市场从沃什的表态及经济数据中推断10月连续加息概率较高，其后副主席们相继发声纠偏，暗示并不急于再次行动，市场预期随即逆转。 美联储理事Christopher Waller将这一插曲形容为大幅压缩前瞻指引的局限性，称此举无异于"倒洗澡水时把孩子也一起倒掉" ，并直言： 我想不出有什么比那一周发生的事情更像前瞻指引了。 前美联储副主席Donald Kohn 表示，在向市场发出如此大的信号之前，他过去会先把讲话内容分享给时任主席格林斯潘或伯南克，征询意见。 他表示，两人从未表示过异议。Kohn说： 当前事态表明，至少部分委员会成员对如此匮乏的前瞻指引感到不安，因为市场正在走到委员会希望引导的方向之前。 委员会缺乏共识，乱象或将延续 令这一状况更为复杂的是，当前官员们不仅对经济形势判断存在分歧，也对政策路径未能形成统一叙事。 文章指出，部分官员认为货币政策明显偏松；另一些人则将此轮加息更多视为对多年高通胀固化价格预期这一风险的保险性应对。 瑞银首席美国经济学家Jonathan Pingle表示，在正常情况下，主席的表态可以为其他官员提供可以援引的共同语言，由主席代表委员会发言"能够带来某种连贯性，而我认为这正是目前所欠缺的"。 前美联储经济学家Claudia Sahm将当前局面概括为"所有可能结果中最坏的一种"。她说： 没有人能强迫他为委员会发言，而坦率地说，他也无法强迫其他委员会成员闭嘴。 目前，一支由外部专家组成的工作组正在就美联储沟通方式起草建议，预计年底前提交。沃什表示，任何调整均须经由全体委员会决定。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 中选之后 美国股市可能将遭受巨大压力
articles.summary: 一周后的美国中期选举，华尔街表面上风平浪静，VIX在19附近晃荡，基金经理们嘴里念叨着一个统计数据：1946年以来，中选后12个月标普500从未下跌。像念护身符一样。 但护身符有个前提：以前美股从来没有在席勒CAPE逼近41倍、十年期美债收益率站上5%、AI资本开支占GDP 2%、前十大成分股吃掉指数一半权重的时候，去迎接一次国会易手。 这一次民主党拿下众院的概率超过九成，横扫两院的概率在六成左右。

articles.title: M6芯片加持！新款苹果iMac AI性能直接翻5倍，起售价12499元
articles.summary: 苹果公司本周密集发布新品， 在触控屏MacBook Pro亮相前夕，率先推出搭载M6芯片的24英寸iMac与14英寸入门级MacBook Pro。 两款新机将于10月29日凌晨1点10分接受预购，11月6日正式发货。 新款iMac起售价12499元人民币，MacBook Pro起售价15999元。 苹果表示， M6芯片赋予新款iMac在人工智能任务上较上代机型五倍的性能提升 ，入门级MacBook Pro的图形处理速度则较前代提升30%。 此次发布是苹果本周新品攻势的第二波，周一该公司刚更新了iPad mini，新增屏幕升级与防水功能。 华尔街见闻提及 ，苹果将于周三以其史上首款触控屏MacBook Pro为本周产品发布收尾。 M6芯片成核心升级，外观延续前代设计 新款iMac与MacBook Pro在外观上与前代产品高度相似，主要变化集中于内部硬件。两款机型均搭载M6芯片——该芯片于今年9月随Mac mini首次亮相。 此次更新中，iMac从M4芯片跨代升级至M6，而MacBook Pro去年刚搭载了M5芯片，本次迭代周期相对更短。 在连接性方面，两款新机均支持蓝牙6与WiFi 7，新款MacBook Pro还获得更快的充电速度。 苹果目前仍继续销售搭载M5 Pro与M5 Max芯片的高端MacBook Pro机型，后者在主处理器与图形核心规格上均高于本次发布的入门级M6机型。 苹果本周三将发布史上首款配备触控屏的MacBook Pro，终结该公司对触控屏笔记本长达二十余年的抵制立场。 新款触控屏MacBook Pro将采用更轻薄的机身设计、更窄的屏幕边框，并引入OLED显示技术。 苹果电脑产品线换代路线图延伸至2028年 此轮密集更新是苹果更宏观产品规划的一部分。 据彭博新闻报道，除触控屏MacBook Pro外， 苹果还计划于明年上半年推出焕新版MacBook Neo与MacBook Air。 在芯片路线图方面，苹果预计于2027年发布M7、M7 Pro与M7 Max芯片 ，并推出经过重新设计的入门级MacBook Pro；M7 Ultra芯片与新款Mac Studio则被安排在2028年推出。 苹果正持续推进电脑产品线的全面革新，以满足日益增长的人工智能应用需求，此次发布的两款新品是这一进程中的阶段性节点，而非终点。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: ASM大涨！2027年营收目标上调24%，宣布最高3亿欧元股票回购计划｜财报见闻
articles.summary: ASM International大幅上调明年营收预期，AI基础设施建设带动的旺盛需求正推动这家荷兰芯片设备制造商或将提前三年完成2030年增长目标。 周二， ASM International将2027年营收目标上调约24%至逾57亿欧元（约63亿美元，按固定汇率计算），高于7月份预测的46亿欧元以上。 从盈利表现来看，ASM第三季度营收按固定汇率计算同比增长44%至11.6亿欧元，净利润为3.081亿欧元，两项指标均超出分析师平均预期。 公司同步公布了最高3亿欧元的股票回购计划。 消息公布后，ASM的美国存托凭证大涨7%，报838.9美元。 首席执行官Hichem M'Saad表示，"需求环境依然非常强劲，客户产能持续紧张，并正加速提升产出。" AI数据中心投资潮，推动上下游同步扩张 ASM明年增长的核心动力来自存储芯片及先进逻辑芯片制造商的双重需求拉动，两类芯片均是数据中心运营商建设AI基础设施的关键原材料。 ASM的核心产品为薄膜沉积设备，用于在晶圆表面沉积极薄的功能膜层，是芯片制造流程中的关键工序。随着客户加速扩产并寻求提升芯片效率与性能，ASM正持续赢得更多订单。 ASM的客户群涵盖台积电与英特尔等行业巨头。台积电负责为英伟达和苹果生产芯片，其资本支出计划高达640亿美元；英特尔则预计今年在新厂房及设备上投入约200亿美元。 AI投资浪潮的红利并非ASM独享。同为荷兰芯片设备商的阿斯麦本月早些时候表示，由于当前产能无法满足2027年及2028年的订单需求，公司正积极扩充生产能力。 两家公司的同步景气，折射出全球芯片设备行业在本轮AI资本开支周期中所处的有利位置——核心设备供给偏紧，客户议价空间有限，头部设备商得以主动把握扩产节奏。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.summary: 弗拉维奥·博索纳罗在输掉总统大选后被没收护照，随即疑似出走巴西，巴西政坛随之陷入动荡。 当地时间27日周二，巴西最高法院法官Flávio Dino下令联邦警察展开调查，核查败选候选人弗拉维奥·博索纳罗的总统竞选活动是否存在非法外国资助，涉事方包括一个由美国副总统万斯联合创立的团体Rockbridge Network。Dino强调，此命令并不意味着已认定存在违法行为，但相关指控足以触发调查。 与此同时，博索纳罗被最高法院责令上交护照，据巴西媒体Folha de S.Paulo报道，他在未遵守期限的情况下疑似出走巴西。 万斯的办公室未立即回应置评请求。彭博联系Rockbridge Network联合创始人Christopher Buskirk，对方亦未立即回应。Meta援引此前有关巴西大选的声明，否认在选举中偏袒任何特定候选人；预测市场平台Polymarket未立即回应置评请求。 调查范围：国外资助、算法干预与稀土利益 根据周二公布的法院文件，Dino要求警方核查Rockbridge Network与两名巴西商人之间的接触，以确定是否有资源、服务或其他具有经济价值的利益流入博索纳罗的竞选活动。 调查还延伸至与Polymarket及Meta相关的竞选广告投放，并将审查互联网公司是否存在Dino所描述的蓄意“算法操纵”，或以人为方式制造不对等分发效果来影响选情。 巴西法律明确禁止候选人及政党接受外国实体或政府的金钱或其他经济援助。Dino表示，这一禁令不仅限于直接现金捐款，还涵盖服务及其他利益。 此次调查还将单独审查潜在政治融资与外国对巴西稀土及其他关键矿产经济利益之间是否存在关联。 指控源起：前候选人举报，竞选广告受质疑 调查的直接导火索来自落选候选人Renan Santos的举报。Santos在首轮选举中未能晋级决赛，随后指控Rockbridge Network参与了为博索纳罗竞选活动争取资金支持的谈判。 在Polymarket问题上，Dino要求调查人员查明谁向境外社交媒体账号付费，以发布基于Polymarket预测数据的选举相关内容——Polymarket的服务在巴西属于被禁范畴。调查须厘清资金来源，以及巴西境内人员或机构是否知情参与其中。 在Meta方面，在决赛轮投票前，巴西选举法庭已下令Meta不得干预政治或选举相关内容的分发。卢拉竞选团队指控Meta"反复且系统性地"阻碍其内容触达用户，并称Meta AI在拒绝生成与卢拉相关图片的同时，却为博索纳罗生成竞选素材。Meta表示，技术事故波及了各政治派别的竞选活动，否认偏袒或代表任何候选人进行干预。 护照被没收，博索纳罗疑似出走 在上述调查启动的同时，博索纳罗本人的行踪引发更大关注。最高法院法官Alexandre de Moraes以担忧其存在潜逃风险为由，在博索纳罗面临多项刑事调查期间，下令其在24小时内上交普通护照及外交护照。博索纳罗未能在截止期限前遵从命令，联邦警察随即注销其护照。 据巴西媒体Folha de S.Paulo援引博索纳罗盟友的消息报道，他在输掉大选后数小时内已出走巴西。 博获悉，博索纳罗的盟友周二上午曾尝试与其取得联系，但未获回音。 阿根廷媒体Infobae报道称，博索纳罗经由与巴西接壤的米西奥内斯省进入阿根廷，并计划从那里前往美国，但阿根廷总统哈维尔·米莱的新闻秘书Adrian Ravier在新闻发布会上否认博索纳罗已入境阿根廷，并表示未收到任何庇护申请。 巴西联邦警察亦表示，未发现博索纳罗通过任何官方边境口岸出境的记录，目前正与阿根廷当局保持联系以确认情况。 家族政治遗产与多重调查压力 现年45岁的弗拉维奥·博索纳罗是前总统贾尔·博索纳罗的长子，目前在任参议员，面临至少两项联邦调查。其一涉及与前Banco Master SA所有人Daniel Vorcaro相关的洗钱、腐败及逃税指控，该银行深陷巴西史上最大规模银行欺诈案。博索纳罗否认存在不当行为，但承认曾向Vorcaro寻求资金，用于拍摄一部关于其父的纪录片。其二源于联邦警察的另一项调查，指出他与一名涉嫌洗钱的律师存在关联。 其父贾尔·博索纳罗的经历为此次事件提供了参照背景。贾尔在2022年大选落败后离开巴西前往美国，后虽返回，但被裁定因在选举前散布虚假信息而禁止担任公职八年，并于2025年9月被裁定犯有政变阴谋罪，同年11月被捕，目前正在家中执行为期27年的软禁刑罚。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 波音大跌！737产量目标推迟至明年，自由现金流指引大幅低于市场预期｜财报见闻
articles.summary: 波音公司最新财务披露令市场失望，股价随即大幅下挫。 波音首席执行官Kelly Ortberg周二表示， 公司737系列飞机月产量达到47架的目标将推迟至2027年初，这一时间表较此前预期大幅延后。 与此同时，公司公布的自由现金流增长预期远低于华尔街共识： 明年预计约30亿美元，2028年约60亿美元，而据LSEG数据，分析师此前分别预测为56亿美元和96亿美元。 截至发稿，波音股价大跌10%，触及2025年4月以来低点。 产能目标再度推迟，交付节奏承压 Ortberg在接受CNBC采访时表示，737飞机月产47架的目标原计划于今年夏季实现，现已延至"明年年初"，并由此导致公司今年500架飞机的年度交付目标同样无法完成。 波音今年9月曾披露，公司机翼生产速度不足是制约产能爬坡的关键瓶颈。737系列单通道客机是波音现金流的核心来源，产能迟滞对公司整体财务恢复构成直接影响。 波音同时面临787项目及777货机生产方面的持续挑战。对此，Ortberg表示："我们正在以正确的方式推进产能爬坡。"他同时强调，尽管外部存在加快737增产的压力，"但我们会保持理性和纪律，前景是有的。" 季度业绩逊于预期，商业航空部门亏损收窄 波音三季度调整后每股亏损34美分，高于市场预期的21美分亏损，据LSEG数据显示。 商业航空部门营收小幅下滑至107亿美元，营业亏损6.97亿美元，营业利润率收窄6.5%，但相较于去年同期48.3%的大幅收缩，已显著改善。 公司将这一表现归因于交付机型盈利能力较低以及包括供应链在内的较高生产成本。 值得关注的是，本季度波音获得了737 MAX 7的美国监管认证，并在10月取得了更大机型MAX 10的认证，同时赢得美国海军第六代F/A-XX战斗机合同。 国防与服务部门表现亮眼，提供业绩支撑 相较于商业航空部门的承压，波音国防和航天部门表现明显改善。 得益于较高的交付量、运营效率提升，以及一笔2.52亿美元的子公司出售收益，该部门季度营业利润接近5亿美元，营业利润率升至6.2%，较去年同期的1.7%大幅提升。 波音全球服务部门季度营业利润达10亿美元，营业利润率为18.3%，继续为集团整体贡献稳定盈利来源。 债务压力边际缓解，复苏进程仍任重道远 财务数据显示，波音三季度末净债务约为252亿美元，较上季度的259亿美元小幅下降，亦低于去年同期的304亿美元，债务压力有所缓解。 Ortberg在业绩发布后向员工发出备忘录称："各方预期正在上升，这理所应当。我们比一年前拥有更坚实的基础，但在消化积压订单、强化企业文化、改善日常运营方面，仍有大量工作要做。" 高油价持续推动航司对燃油效率更高机型的需求，但Ortberg也提示这是"需要持续关注的因素"。对于仍背负沉重债务、声誉尚未完全修复的波音而言，产能爬坡的节奏与现金流的恢复速度，将是投资者未来最为关注的核心变量。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 美国房贷利率飙升、购房需求疲软：9月新屋销售环比下降0.6%，房价同比下跌3.9%
articles.summary: 美国新屋市场在房贷利率大幅攀升的压力下继续承压，建筑商降价促销未能有效提振需求。 美国政府周二公布数据显示， 9月新建单户住宅销售环比下降0.6%，折年率为67.6万套，高于彭博调查经济学家预期的65.1万套中位数。 与此同时， 新屋中位售价同比下跌3.9%至40.04万美元，今年已有九个月中的七个月录得同比价格下降。 房贷利率上月上涨约半个百分点，并于10月初触及近三年来最高水平，此后仅小幅回落。 这一融资成本的快速攀升正在侵蚀潜在购房者的购买意愿，并拖累建筑商信心指数跌至14年来最低点。 降价让步难抵利率冲击，市场仍缺乏实质性需求 全美保险公司（Nationwide）经济学家Daniel Vielhaber指出，建筑商正不得不付出更多努力吸引买家，高企的房贷利率料将至少在年底前持续压制销售环境。 "降价和提供房贷利率补贴有助于维持销售运转，但市场更多依赖建筑商让步，而非强劲的内生需求来支撑，" Vielhaber在一份研究报告中表示。 在需求持续疲软的背景下，建筑商去化库存的进度依然迟缓。 9月新屋待售库存较去年同期下降2.3%至47.6万套，以当前销售速度衡量相当于8.4个月的供应量 ——虽为年内最低水平，但仍远高于疫情前的历史常态。 入门级市场承压，建筑商以小户型及利率补贴应对 彭博行业研究分析师Drew Reading上周在研究报告中指出，入门级购房者对融资成本上升尤为敏感，主要服务于这一群体的建筑商，如D.R. Horton Inc.和Meritage Homes Corp.面临更大的风险敞口。 建筑商正竭力维持客户购买意愿，通过提供更小户型住宅及补贴房贷利率等方式来缓解负担能力不足的问题。 值得注意的是，新屋销售数据以合同签订为基准统计，被视为比以成交过户计算的成屋销售更为及时的市场先行指标。但该数据月度波动性较大——政府报告显示，9月新屋销售变动幅度的90%置信区间为下降14.4%至上升13.2%，解读时需保持审慎。 从区域来看，全美最大的新屋销售市场南部地区9月销售折年率下降6.6%至41.3万套，中西部地区销售同样走低，部分抵消了西部和东北部的涨幅。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。
